description: We are FireNova, a team of three university students passionate about software development, data science, and space technology. For this challenge, we aim to develop an interactive solution that combines MODIS and VIIRS satellite hotspot data to improve wildfire monitoring and visualization. We are excited to turn NASA data into meaningful insights through technology, creativity, and teamwork.
summary:
FireNova is a web-based wildfire activity analysis platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our project addresses the challenge of harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire detection data, enabling users to explore historical burning activity through an interactive map and timeline.

One of the main challenges is that MODIS and VIIRS have different detection capabilities, making direct comparisons unreliable. To address this, we processed over 300 million satellite hotspot records, applied sensor calibration and harmonization techniques, and organized the data into monthly geographic grids.

We also implemented a Leave-One-Year-Out (LOYO) anomaly detection method to identify unusually high or low fire activity compared to historical patterns. The results are presented through interactive geographic visualizations, helping users explore regional trends and historical anomalies.

FireNova transforms complex satellite observations into accessible, meaningful insights, supporting researchers, environmental organizations, and emergency management teams in understanding historical fire patterns and improving data-informed decision-making.
details:
FireNova – Project Details

Project Overview

FireNova is an interactive, web-based platform designed to analyze and visualize historical global burning activity using satellite observations from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments.

Our project addresses a major challenge in Earth observation: different satellite sensors detect active fires with different sensitivities and resolutions, making their observations difficult to compare directly.

FireNova brings these datasets together through a harmonization pipeline and transforms millions of satellite observations into an accessible, interactive experience. By combining scientific data processing with intuitive visualizations, our platform helps users understand when and where burning activity has occurred, how it has changed over time, and whether observed activity is unusual compared to historical patterns.

How FireNova Works

FireNova consists of three main components: satellite data processing, historical anomaly detection, and interactive visualization.

1. Satellite Data Processing and Harmonization

We collected and processed more than 300 million active fire hotspot records from NASA FIRMS, including observations from MODIS and VIIRS instruments aboard multiple satellites.

Because MODIS and VIIRS have different detection characteristics, directly combining their raw hotspot counts could introduce misleading trends.

To address this challenge, we developed a Python-based processing pipeline that:

  • Cleans and standardizes satellite observations.
  • Organizes fire detections into geographic grids of 2° × 2°.
  • Aggregates hotspot observations into monthly activity records.
  • Calculates calibration factors using overlapping MODIS and VIIRS observations.
  • Produces a harmonized historical dataset for consistent analysis.
  • Identifies missing observations and distinguishes them from verified measurements.

This approach reduces sensor-related inconsistencies while preserving important information about historical burning activity.

2. Historical Anomaly Detection

Beyond displaying fire detections, FireNova helps users understand whether burning activity in a particular region and month is unusual.

We implemented a statistical anomaly detection approach based on the Leave-One-Year-Out (LOYO) method.

For each geographic grid and calendar month, the system compares the selected year's activity with observations from other available years. This allows us to identify unusually high or low activity relative to historical patterns.

The platform classifies results into categories such as:

  • Very High Activity
  • High Activity
  • Normal Activity
  • Low Activity
  • Very Low Activity
  • Insufficient Data

We also account for historical data availability and uncertainty to avoid presenting missing observations as confirmed periods without fire activity.

Importantly, these anomalies represent historical statistical deviations, not predictions of future wildfires.

3. Interactive User Interface and Visualization

A central part of FireNova is its interactive web interface, designed to make complex satellite data understandable to users without requiring advanced technical knowledge.

Interactive Globe and Geographic Exploration

The application features an interactive 3D globe that allows users to explore geographic regions and investigate historical burning activity.

Instead of presenting millions of individual satellite detections, FireNova organizes observations into geographic cells, making regional patterns easier to explore and interpret.

Timeline and Historical Exploration

Users can explore burning activity across different years and months, examining how patterns change over time.

The historical timeline helps reveal seasonal variations, recurring burning periods, and changes in regional activity.

Burning Activity Calendar

The calendar-oriented visualization provides a structured way to examine monthly burning patterns and identify periods with unusually high or low activity.

This helps users understand not only where burning activity occurs, but also when it becomes more prominent.

Regional Data and Anomaly Visualization

By examining geographic cells, users can access historical activity information and anomaly classifications.

The interface connects geographic exploration with time-based analysis, making it easier to investigate specific regions and compare historical conditions.

Visual Design and Accessibility

We designed FireNova with an emphasis on clear navigation, visual hierarchy, and intuitive interaction.

Our goal was to transform large and complex scientific datasets into meaningful visual information, allowing users to explore patterns without needing to interpret raw satellite files or perform statistical calculations themselves.

Technologies and Development Tools

FireNova combines data engineering, statistical analysis, and modern web development.

Data Processing and Analysis

  • Python for data cleaning, aggregation, harmonization, and anomaly detection.
  • DuckDB and Pandas for efficient processing and analysis of large datasets.
  • CSV and JSON formats for storing and transferring processed data.
  • Custom validation scripts for checking data consistency, completeness, and processing accuracy.

Frontend Development

  • React for building the interactive user interface.
  • TypeScript for structured and maintainable frontend development.
  • Vite for frontend development and production builds.
  • Web-based 3D visualization for interactive geographic exploration.

Development and Collaboration

  • Git and GitHub for version control, team collaboration, and integration.
  • Visual Studio Code and local development environments.
  • Automated validation scripts and production build checks.

The project was developed using standard personal computers, demonstrating that large-scale satellite data analysis can be made accessible without requiring specialized computing hardware.

What Makes FireNova Creative?

FireNova goes beyond traditional wildfire maps that primarily display individual fire detections or recent events.

Our innovation lies in combining multi-sensor harmonization, historical anomaly analysis, and interactive geographic storytelling within a single platform.

Rather than simply showing where satellites detected fires, FireNova provides historical context for those observations.

A region with high burning activity may be experiencing a typical seasonal pattern, while another region with fewer detections may be experiencing an unusually active period compared to its own history.

FireNova helps users explore this distinction.

The integration of an interactive globe, geographic grids, historical timelines, and anomaly classifications creates a more informative experience than displaying raw hotspot locations alone.

Additionally, our processing pipeline converts hundreds of millions of raw detections into structured data that can be explored efficiently through a browser.

Challenges and Design Considerations

Throughout development, our team focused on several important technical and scientific challenges.

Sensor Differences: MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions and detection capabilities. We addressed this through calibration and harmonization rather than assuming their raw measurements were directly equivalent.

Large Data Volumes: Processing more than 300 million records required efficient data handling, aggregation, and structured exports.

Missing Data: Missing satellite observations do not necessarily mean that no fires occurred. We therefore introduced explicit handling for uncertain or unverified observations.

Scientific Reliability: We developed automated validation procedures to verify the integrity of processed records, anomaly classifications, sensor transitions, and frontend exports.

Performance and Usability: We organized the processed information into annual datasets and geographic JSON files to support efficient retrieval and interactive exploration.

Data Interpretation: Active fire hotspot counts are not equivalent to burned area, fire intensity, or fire severity. Our platform is designed to communicate historical detection activity rather than make unsupported claims about fire damage.

Geographic Coverage: Although the platform uses a global geographic interface, the analyzed observations are limited to the geographic coverage of the datasets included in our processing pipeline.

These considerations helped us balance scientific accuracy, computational efficiency, and user experience.

Intended Impact and Benefits

FireNova aims to make historical satellite fire observations more accessible, comparable, and useful.

For researchers, it provides a way to investigate seasonal burning patterns and historical anomalies.

For environmental organizations and land managers, it offers a clearer perspective on how burning activity varies across regions and time.

For emergency management and monitoring teams, historical patterns can provide valuable context when evaluating periods of increased fire activity and planning monitoring priorities.

For students and the general public, FireNova provides an approachable way to explore Earth observation data and understand the role of satellites in environmental monitoring.

By reducing the complexity of multi-sensor datasets and presenting historical information through an interactive interface, FireNova helps bridge the gap between satellite science and practical understanding.

Conclusion

FireNova transforms fragmented satellite fire observations into a harmonized, interactive historical burning activity platform.

By combining NASA MODIS and VIIRS data, statistical anomaly detection, and accessible geographic visualization, our project demonstrates how Earth observation data can be used to reveal meaningful environmental patterns.

Our ultimate goal is to support better-informed research, environmental awareness, and decision-making by making historical burning activity easier to explore, compare, and understand.
